20248-the-necessity-of-atheism:
The Necessity of Atheism, in this 1933 printing, argues that gods began in human fear. To early man, the gods were as real as mountains and waterfalls. Spirits in drugs and wines seemed facts of the same order. Their power to heal or intoxicate proved their presence, men thought.

From such roots, the book traces belief toward doubt and reason. Its title echoes Shelley's famed student tract of the same name. Arguments cover nature, scripture, and the harm of forced belief. Readers get a blunt, clear case for unbelief from the freethought tradition.
20428-bertha-and-her-baptism:
Bertha and Her Baptism is a religious story written to teach young readers about baptism and heaven. It opens with a claim its makers held dear. Of those who have gone to heaven from this world, by far the larger part, it says, have been infants and young children.

The teaching runs through the tale of Bertha herself. Born sinners by one man's disobedience, children are born again of the Spirit, the book explains. Its early move to heaven is treated as mercy, not loss. Stories like this one filled Victorian nurseries, where faith and comfort were taught together.
21853-woman-s-work-in-the-civil-war-a-re:
Women's war work fills this 1867 record by L. P. Brockett and Mary C. Vaughan, gathered as the Civil War still raged. The gathering began in the autumn of 1863, out of a small book on the war's kind results meant for readers abroad. Henry W. Bellows of the Sanitary Commission writes the introduction. Sixteen steel engravings honor the women inside, Clara Barton among them.

The subtitle promises heroism, patriotism, and patience, and the pages deliver all three. Nurses, aid workers, teachers of freed people, and women who kept homes and farms appear in turn. Barbara Frietchie's famous defiance fronts the book. It stands as an early monument to the women the war made visible, written while their work was fresh.
21991-face-to-face-with-kaiserism:
James W. Gerard, lately America's ambassador to the German imperial court, continues his account in Face to Face with Kaiserism, published in 1918. The book follows his bestseller My Four Years in Germany, carrying the story to his return home. Gerard dedicates it to Colonel Edward M. House, statesman and friend. Facsimiles fill the plates: the Kaiser's visiting card, prison camp money, and stamps from Ruhleben camp.

Gerard shows the paper money used in prison camps and issued against German property. His subject is the system he faced for four years: the Kaiser, his court, and the machine behind them. Written while the war still raged, it is diplomacy as testimony. Gerard writes for American readers deciding what Germany under the Kaiser truly was.
22147-peter-the-hermit-a-tale-of-enthusi:
Daniel A. Goodsell, a Methodist bishop, wrote Peter the Hermit: A Tale of Enthusiasm in 1906. Peter was the ragged preacher whose sermons fired the First Crusade. Goodsell opens in the Holy Land of pilgrims' longing. The devout Christian, he writes, dreams of walking where the Master walked and praying in the garden of his agony.

From that longing Goodsell's Peter gathers his ragged army. The tale follows the march of the People's Crusade toward Jerusalem and its ruin. Goodsell treats Peter neither as saint nor fraud, but as enthusiasm made flesh. His book is part history, part sermon, aimed at church readers who loved the Crusades' great names.
22283-mind-and-motion-and-monism:
George John Romanes, Darwin's younger friend and defender, wrote Mind and Motion and Monism near the end of his life. The book appeared in 1895, after his death. Romanes quotes the old materialist claim that our feelings are only motions of matter pressing on our organs. Motion, that doctrine says, produces nothing but motion, and mind must be explained away or explained by it.

Romanes refuses the easy answer. Trained as a biologist and drawn to philosophy, he argues toward monism: mind and matter as two sides of one reality. The book joins his work on animal intelligence to the deepest question he knew. It is Victorian science thinking hard about the soul.
a-guide-to-stoicism:
St. George Stock, of Pembroke College, Oxford, wrote A Guide to Stoicism as a small handbook, issued in the Ten Cent Pocket Series edited by E. Haldeman-Julius. His foreword strips the subject to a claim: remove the paradoxes and the wilful misuse of language. Stoicism is the moral philosophy of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, dashed with the physics of Heraclitus.

The guide sketches philosophy among Greeks and Romans, then the Stoic doctrine itself, drawn from the original authorities rather than handbooks. Logic, nature, fate, and the rule of living by reason are set out in short order for a general reader. It aims at the pocket and the railway journey: ancient philosophy made portable without being made shallow.
an-essay-on-criticism:
Alexander Pope published An Essay on Criticism in 1711, when he was barely into his twenties, and the hosted edition adds a life of the poet plus introductory and explanatory notes. The life recalls his Catholic schooling, his self-teaching after age twelve, and the Twickenham villa from which he became the most popular poet of his age.

The poem itself, in heroic couplets, lays down how to read, judge, and write: follow nature, study the ancients, and distrust pride and petty rules. Famous lines on little learning and on pardoning faults have been quoted ever since. With the notes around it, the edition serves a new reader twice over, giving both the poem and a guided way into Pope's critical world.
b09-luther-large-catechism:
Martin Luther published the Large Catechism in 1529 for pastors and teachers who had to instruct whole parishes. A catechism teaches faith by question and answer, and Luther's large one treats each part at full length. It covers the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, baptism, and the Lord's Supper.

Luther writes with force and warmth, urging teachers never to think they have learned enough. His preface scolds lazy pastors in terms still quoted today. The book became a fixed standard of Lutheran teaching, kept among its confessional texts. Churches have used it to train clergy ever since. Few teaching books of the age match its plain strength.
b09-luther-small-catechism:
The Small Catechism of 1529 was Martin Luther's handbook for the home, his Enchiridion for heads of households. Where the Large Catechism served pastors, this small one fits in a hand and a memory. It gives the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer in short form.

Baptism, confession, and the Lord's Supper follow, each with brief, clear answers to set questions. Morning and evening prayers and a Table of Duties for each place in life close the book. Luther meant fathers to teach it at table, week by week. It became the most printed Lutheran text after the Bible, and children still learn it today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adoptionism:
Adoptionism is a christological theory holding Christ as man God's adoptive Son, though its precise import varies by stage. Roughly there are three forms. First, Elipandus and Felix's eighth-century Adoptionism. Second, Abelard's twelfth-century Neo-Adoptionism. Third, the qualified Adoptionism of later theologians.

The original form asserts Christ's double sonship: one by generation and nature, and one by adoption and grace. As God, Christ is Son by generation and nature, but as man he is Son only by adoption and grace. Elipandus, Archbishop of Toledo under Mohammedan rule, and Felix, Bishop of Urgel under Frankish dominion, held this theory late in the eighth century. Its origin is obscure. Nestorianism was an Eastern heresy, yet an offshoot appeared in the far west, where a Nestorian colony had found refuge in Islamic Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnosticism:
Agnosticism is a philosophical theory of knowledge's limits, professing doubt or disbelief about what the mind can know, in part or whole. The word Agnostic, from Greek a, privative, plus gnostikos, knowing, comes from Professor Huxley in 1869. It described one who saw all attempts to know the reality behind ultimate scientific, philosophic, and religious ideas as futile.

Huxley contrasted his own unpretentious ignorance with the vain knowledge claimed by second- and third-century Gnostics. That antithesis, the entry argues, was unfair and overdrawn, serving to discredit natural theology by classing it with Gnostic vapourings. Rather, Gnostic and Agnostic are the real extremists. The former stretches knowledge's bounds unduly, the latter narrows them. Natural theology, or theism, holds the middle ground between claiming the mind can know everything and claiming it can know nothing about religious truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agrarianism:
Agrarianism takes its name from Latin agrarius, applied historically to laws or their supporters favouring division of Roman public lands among poorer citizens. So agrarianism and agrarian in English generally imply theories and movements meant to benefit poorer classes by dealing somehow with land ownership or farmers' legal duties. In German, Agrar means rural, and the Agrarpartei matches England's former country party.

Keeping to the stricter use, two social movements running through history stand out: agrarian reform and agrarian revolution. Conspicuous among reforms is the Hebrew Prophets' case. How far the Mosaic Law's land system ever fully worked is disputed, probably unascertainable; ascertainable is the growth, alongside wealth and commerce under the kings, of Hebrew peasantry ill-treatment. Over-taxation for a luxurious court, corn-jobbery and monopoly, and usurious loans made the peasant a debtor-slave or dispossessed him entirely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alcoholism:
Alcoholism, as this entry uses the term, covers every change alcohol can bring about in the human body. These range from brief exhilaration to deep unconsciousness, coma, and even death. The effects vary with the amount taken, the form of alcohol, how fast it is given, and how used the person is to it. Alcohol itself is about ninety-one per cent ethyl alcohol by weight and nine per cent water.

The entry follows alcohol through the body. All vital processes play out inside the cell., and nearly all alcohol taken passes from the stomach into the blood and straight to the liver by the portal vein. It then considers the effects on organs and tissues, including the skin, where alcohol excites a sense of heat. Physiologists agree on the facts of alcohol's action, the entry notes, but differ sharply on the conclusions to draw from them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altruism:
Altruism is a term Auguste Comte formed in 1851 from the Italian altrui, for benevolent as against selfish propensities. George H. Lewes brought it into English in 1853, and Comte's expounders popularized it. Psychologically it names reflective emotions benefiting others, but its important sense is ethical.

Comte's religious system won few adherents, too extravagant even for Littré, one of his earliest able followers. Catholic teaching sums love of others in Christ's precept, love thy neighbour as thyself, with self-love as exemplar but not measure. Catholic ethics reconciles self-love and benevolence under creation's supreme purpose, allowing self-love moral quality and subordinating both to the Creator's ends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anglicanism:
Anglicanism denotes the belief and position of the established Church of England and communicating churches in British lands, the United States, and elsewhere. It includes those who accepted the English Reformation as embodied in the Church of England or in offshoot churches adhering to its doctrines and liturgy. Apart from minor settlements, its area matches lands under the British flag.

The article sketches Anglicanism in the Established Church in three periods. Henry VIII's reign was ostensibly conservative, aiming at a Catholic Church minus the pope, yet his actions contradicted him. The Edwardian and Elizabethan periods carried separation further. In belief, Anglicans accept Scripture as containing all things necessary to salvation, take the Prayer Book as the rule of worship, and recognize Baptism and the Lord's Supper. The clergy subscribe the Thirty-nine Articles. Three schools divide Anglican thought: Low, Broad, and High Church, culminating in the Oxford Movement of 1833.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-animism:
Animism, from Latin anima, soul, is the theory of the soul. In current language it has a twofold meaning. Philosophically, it holds the soul to be life's principle in man and other living things. For man, it embodies spiritualistic philosophy as opposed to materialistic philosophy. Animism seeks knowledge of man's nature, establishing the soul's existence, nature, union with the body, origin, and duration. These problems underlie conscious existence and mental and moral studies.

Ethnologically, it is a recent theory of religion's origin, the ghost theory. At bottom it is a biological theory, explaining phenomena by living analogy. To primitive man, all moving things lived, and ghost fancy soon extended to all objects. Spiritual beings are modelled on man's own soul. Burial customs illustrate it: horses and camels slain at graves, food and weapons in tombs, surviving in paper messengers burned and substitutes on graves in China and Japan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthropomorph:
Anthropomorphism, from anthropos, man, and morphe, form, means man pictures the outer world's acts as his own. A system built on this bent is called philosophic. But most often it means that bent at work in faith. In faith, it gives the Supreme Being human form, limbs, operations, and traits.

This bent shows strongly in primitive heathen faiths and in all polytheism, especially in Greek and Roman pagan worship. Xenophanes of Colophon charged the Greeks with it. The first Christian apologists blamed pagans for showing God in human form. Throughout the Fathers, God's spirituality, and man's weak grasp of His boundless perfection, are stressed again and again. Yet Catholic philosophy forms its idea of God from our own minds and moral characteristics, while noting all made good falls far short of God's own good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antinomianism:
Antinomianism, anti, against, and nomos, law, holds Christians free from moral law. The term arose in Luther's day for Agricola's teachings. Pushing faith-alone to a logical conclusion, Agricola held good works do not promote salvation, nor evil works hinder it. Justified Christians, he held, cannot lose holiness or their saved state by disobedience or violation of God's law.

After doubtful standing among slanderers warned against by the Apostle, Antinomianism came back as a variant of Protestant faith doctrine early in the German Reformation. It set Luther and his disciple and fellow townsman Agricola, born at Eisleben in 1492, at odds. The doctrine is mostly held in theory, seldom urged in practice, and was banned by the Council of Trent's decree on Justification, whose fifteenth chapter concerns this heresy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apollinariani:
Apollinarianism is a Christological theory, a teaching about the nature of Christ. It holds that he had a human body and a human feeling soul, but no human rational mind, with the divine Logos, or Word, taking the mind's place. Its author, Apollinaris the Younger, bishop of Laodicea, was active in the later fourth century. He was first highly esteemed by Athanasius, Basil, and Jerome for learning, biblical knowledge, and loyalty to the Nicene faith.

With his father, Apollinaris the Elder, he recast Scripture on classical models to make up for Greek literature lost when Julian's edict barred Christians from teaching it. Jerome credits him with countless volumes on Scripture, two defences of Christianity, and a refutation of Eunomius, but those works are lost. Surviving tracts on his theory, some circulated under false names, let readers see how the church answered a teaching that denied Christ a full human mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arianism:
Arianism, a heresy that arose in the fourth century and rejected the divinity of Jesus Christ, ranks first among disputes that troubled Christians after Constantine recognized the church in 313. It fathered many more over three centuries. It will seem strange to modern eyes, since it is not modern unbelief but an eastern attempt to rationalize the creed.

In the New Testament and church teaching Jesus appears as Son of God, a name he took to himself. John's gospel calls him the Word, or Logos, who existed with God from the beginning and was God, maker of all things. Paul's genuine letters to Ephesians, Colossians, and Philippians lay down a like doctrine. Arianism, denying that full divinity, forced the church to define what it meant by Son and Word, and the entry follows that long definition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arminianism:
Arminianism is the popular name for doctrines held by a party formed early in the seventeenth century among Calvinists of the Netherlands. Human reason, the article argues, revolted against Calvin's horrible decree of absolute predestination. Salvation and damnation were dealt out without regard to merit, and opposition stirred from the dogma's first promulgation. While religious wars gripped the masses, thoughtful minds were few and uninfluential, and Calvin's tenets, the article charges, banished charity and mercy and bred strife and bloodshed.

Calm deliberation could not sustain that spirit, and a leader was sure to rise from Calvinist ranks to expose the Genevan creed's harmful corollaries. That leader was Jacobus Arminius, born Jakob Hermanzoon at Oudewater and professor at Leyden University. The entry follows his teaching, its clash with strict Calvinism, and the party that took his name into the churches of Holland and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asceticism:
Asceticism comes from Greek askesis, meaning practice, bodily exercise, and above all athletic training. Early Christians adopted it for the practice of spiritual things, or spiritual exercises performed to gain habits of virtue. Today it is often used scornfully for religious practices of eastern fanatics as well as Christian saints, lumped together by some. It is often confused with austerity, even by Catholics, but wrongly, the article argues.

Though flesh lusts against spirit and repression and self-denial are needed to control animal passions, virtue cannot be measured by the extent of bodily penances. External penances even in saints are viewed with suspicion. Jerome, prone to austerity himself and therefore a valuable witness, is cited on that caution. The long article separates disciplined training from mere harshness, tracing ascetic practice through scripture, fathers, and saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atavism:
Atavism, from Latin atavus, a great-grandfather's grandfather or ancestor, is a term Duchesne introduced for cases where species revert spontaneously to presumably long-lost characters. Most authors use atavism and reversion in the same sense. The term expresses the reappearance, in individual or race, of physical or psychical traits supposed once held by remote ancestors.

Very often such reappearing traits are monstrous, for example the three-toed horse, whose condition is read as harking back to Tertiary times, when the modern horse's ancestor held three toes. The use of the term in teratology, the study of monstrosities, is often abused, the article warns. Many so-called atavistic monstrosities bear little relation to lost characters, such as extra human digits. The entry separates genuine reversion from loose labelling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atheism:
Atheism, from a privative and theos, God, meaning without God, is the system of thought formally opposed to theism, belief in God. Since first use the term has been employed very vaguely, generally as an accusation against any system questioning the popular gods of the day. Socrates was accused of atheism, Diagoras was called atheist by Cicero, and Democritus and Epicurus were styled impious, without respect for gods, for their new atomistic philosophy.

In the same sense early Christians were known to pagans as atheists because they denied heathen gods, and various religious and philosophical systems have likewise been deemed atheistic. Historically, atheism has often meant no more than critical or sceptical rejection of the theology of those using the term as a charge. The long article moves from that loose label to formal atheism as a system, its arguments, and the Catholic reply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atomism:
Atomism holds that every body is built from minute, indivisible particles called atoms. Leucippus began the philosophy, and his pupil Democritus, born about 460 BC, gave it its classic shape. For Democritus, atoms are eternal and countless, and differences among things come from their size, shape, and place. Epicurus added a slight swerve to falling atoms, and Lucretius defended the theory in verse.

After a long gap, Gassendi revived Epicurean atomism in the 1600s and tried to fit it with Christian belief. The entry then weighs the scientific form against scholastic critics, who read chemical change as a deep change of substance. For those critics, a formula shows how elements react, not a building made of fixed atoms. It ends by calling broad claims about radioactivity premature, since the science of the day could not yet settle the question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptism:
Baptism is one of the Church's seven sacraments, often called the first sacrament and the door of the Church. The entry treats it under many heads, from doctrine and etymology to matter, form, minister, and ceremonies. It opens with two authoritative documents, chiefly Eugene IV's Decree for the Armenians in the bull Exultate Deo. That decree calls baptism the door of spiritual life, making us members of Christ and of the Church.

Substitutes, rebaptism, unbaptized infants, and the sacrament's effects are also treated. Closing sections treat metaphorical baptisms, such as the blessing of bells and of ships. Bells, washed with holy water and anointed inside and out, are blessed to rout demons, guard against storms, and call prayer. Ships have been blessed since Crusader times, recalling Noah's ark and Peter sinking in the sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benthamism:
Benthamism, the philosophy of Jeremy Bentham, receives a critical entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Bentham, an English jurist born in London in 1748, left the bar in disgust at legal chicanery and spent his life rethinking law. Locke, Hume, Montesquieu, and Beccaria shaped his turn to the principles of legislation.

His test was utility: the greatest happiness of the greatest number, judged by pleasures and pains. The entry follows that test through law, punishment, and government, then weighs it against Catholic moral teaching. It finds the calculus clever but thin on duty, rights, and the higher goods of human life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-crit:
Biblical criticism in its textual sense, the recovery of a lost original text, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. It differs from higher criticism, which studies sources, date, and influence. Textual work applies only where the author's own manuscript is gone, since a surviving autograph could simply be photographed or reprinted.

No two hand copies of a long work ever agree in every detail, as the Augsburg Confession of 1530 shows: thirty-five copies made within months already differ, and its originals are lost. The entry explains collation, manuscripts, and versions as the tools for rebuilding the Bible's text as closely as scholarship allows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-birds-in-symb:
Birds in symbolism, the Christian meanings given to birds, receive a charming entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The dove leads, standing for the Holy Spirit, who descended like a dove at Jesus's baptism, and for peace, since a dove brought Noah an olive branch when the flood ended. Early art painted apostles and faithful as doves.

Other birds follow, each with a moral: the eagle for renewal and lofty sight, the pelican for self-giving love, the phoenix for resurrection. The entry gathers Scripture, art, and bestiary lore into a small aviary of faith. It shows how the Church read nature as a picture book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brahminism:
Brahminism, the religion and social system grown from Aryan nature worship in northern India, survives in its modern form as Hinduism. Its earliest sacred books, first spoken then written between 1500 and 400 before Christ, begin with four Vedas. They hold hymns of the Rig-Veda, the Sama-Veda's song-service, the Yajur-Veda's liturgy, and the Atharva-Veda's spells and charms.

Brahmanas explain Vedic rites, Upanishads ponder deity and man's end, and Sutras guide daily rites and law, crowned by the Laws of Manu. Later sections trace early Vedism's many nature gods, popular worship, pantheistic thought, early and sectarian Hinduism, and reform movements. The entry thus maps a faith from simple polytheism to a vast, intricate system still alive today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buddhism:
Buddhism, a religious and monastic system founded about 500 before Christ, grew from pantheistic Brahminism through the Vedanta school's search for release. Vedanta thinkers shared a gloomy view that conscious life is a burden, with happiness only in dreamless, desire-free sleep, and they accepted rebirth's endless chain. Breaking with Vedic rites, they sought escape from rebirth and conscious being, and Buddhism won the greatest fame among these rival paths.

Its founder, Gotama, son of a petty raja on Nepal's southern border, learned the Vedas, married young, and kept a prince's household before worldly pleasures palled. He left home for forest austerity, nearly died of fasting, and turned to long meditation, believing he had found the sole path from rebirth's misery to Nirvana. Preaching first at Benares, his earnest eloquence won warriors and Brahmins alike to his gospel of deliverance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calvinism:
Calvinism takes its shape from Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion, never replaced by any creed, though Calvin signed the Augsburg Confession at Worms in 1540. Coming after Luther, he fought Zwingli's followers at Zurich, who leaned toward a Christianity without mysteries. In 1549 he joined Bullinger in the Consensus of Zurich, a middle view of the Eucharist. A compact of Geneva's pastors in 1552 backed him against Jerome Bolsec on predestination; he refuted Bolsec and jailed him.

Later Eucharist disputes drew Calvin toward Melanchthon's party. Beza softened Geneva's doctrine toward the Lutherans, and the many creeds faded as the Institutes stood as the sum of Reformed theology. Three currents have run through this Protestant growth ever since: mystic from Wittenberg, logical and orthodox from Geneva, and heterodox and rationalist from Zurich. In church life each member must sign formulas, submit to discipline, and be ruled by elders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrism:
An entry on chrism, the mixture of olive oil and balsam blessed by a bishop and used in sacraments and sacred functions. For Confirmation to be valid, the chrism must be pure olive oil blessed by a bishop, or by a priest deputed by the Holy See. Probably it should also contain balsam and receive a blessing distinct from those of the oil of the sick and the oil of catechumens. If those last conditions fail, the sacrament stands doubtfully valid.

Chrism first meant any smearing stuff, but the Fathers narrowed it to the sacred oil of Baptism and Confirmation. Origen speaks of the visible chrism of baptism, and Cyril of Jerusalem praises the mystic chrism. Early councils treat it as set apart for sanctifying men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collectivism:
John Augustine Ryan's entry defines collectivism as a later and more precise term than socialism. Socialism is often used loosely, even for single-tax plans or state ownership of railways and telegraphs. Collectivism is scarcely used except for one system. In it, the public owns and manages the material means of production. It usually marks only the economic side of socialism. It carries no set philosophy, psychology, ethics, or history of its own.

Ryan allows wide variety in how the system might work. He notes that many old arguments against it have lost force as its theory grew clearer. The entry closes near official Catholic teaching. A pope declared that human welfare demands private ownership of stable possessions and of lucrative property, a limit that pure economic collectivism must face.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communism:
John Augustine Ryan's entry defines communism in a broad and a strict sense. Broadly it covers any system where the group owns all property, or at least all productive property, instead of individuals. That sweep takes in communistic anarchism, socialism, and strict communism. Anarchists of this school would end both private property and government. Socialism claims only the material means of production. Strict communism claims consumption goods too: dwellings, furniture, food, and clothing, all held by the whole community.

History opens with Crete near 1300 B.C., then the first Christians of Jerusalem, then medieval heretical sects. French writers of the eighteenth century rebuilt society in theory, and Cabet's Voyage en Icarie of 1840 followed More's model. American experiments fill the later pages: Ephrata, the Shakers, the Harmonists of 1805, the Separatists of Zoar, Oneida, some thirty Fourierist phalanxes of the 1840s, and the Amana community of 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confucianism:
Charles Francis Aiken's entry defines Confucianism as the moral, social, political, and religious system Confucius built on ancient Chinese tradition, kept as state religion. It aims to form the virtuous, learned man of good manners. The perfect man joins saint, scholar, and gentleman. It is a religion without positive revelation, with minimal dogma. Popular worship centers on offerings to the dead. Duty stretches beyond morals into daily life's details.

Confucius, K'ung-tze or K'ung-fu-tze, latinized by Jesuit missionaries, was born in 551 B.C. in a feudal state. Aiken treats teacher, texts, and doctrine in turn. Texts include History, Songs, Changes, Rites with the Doctrine of the Mean and Great Learning, and Mencius. Jesuit researches first opened these books to the West. Aiken closes contrasting Confucian rites, polygamy, and seclusion of women with Christian civilization.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregationa:
James Loughlin's entry traces Congregationalism from Anglican bishops' rule and Catholic rites that offended Protestants, which bred many Puritan factions of varying radicalism. Elizabeth and the Stuarts enforced conformity by force. Timid Puritans stayed in the State Church, protesting popish leanings to the present day. Advanced leaders saw no place in a church ruled by bishops and tied to civil power. Geneva seemed Christ's kingdom on earth, and Scotland drew them toward Presbyterian-style churches.

Many then pressed further, forming independent churches on congregational lines. New England colonies proved decisive for the movement, whose American Puritans preferred the term Congregationalism. Its order holds that the elect, called one by one by the Lord through word and Spirit, walk together in particular societies or churches. Doctrine stayed mostly strict Calvinist. Churches thrived best under persecution's glue; once it lifted, loose order left them open. Congregational unions later answered that weakness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congruism:
Walter McDonald's entry defines Congruism, theologians' term for a theory on efficacious grace. Efficacy owes, at least in part, to grace given in favorable circumstances, hence congruous. Augustine already distinguished gratia congrua from gratia incongrua, calling the elect congruenter vocati in his reply to Simplicianus, book one, question two. Jesuit theologians developed the system at the close of the sixteenth century and the start of the seventeenth.

All Molinists identify actual grace with supernatural action. Actual grace of will, technically inspiration, is an act of will. It begins necessarily and may become free at a point in its duration. The live question follows: why, of two motions similar in constitution, does one prove efficacious and the other not? Motives sway the will, and Molinists hold that before grace, sufficient or efficacious, God knows by scientia media whether it will result. Billuart and other opponents of Molinism pressed the contrary reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creationism:
This doctrinal entry sorts out three meanings of creationism. In the widest sense it is the doctrine that God made the material of the universe from no prior subject, against all forms of pantheism. Less widely, it holds that living species were directly created by God, not produced by evolution. In its restricted and usual sense, it concerns the human soul alone.

That third sense is the entry's real subject. It argues that the soul, being spiritual and indivisible, cannot come from parents by generation or emanate from God. It must be immediately created by God. The entry weighs rival views, including Traducianism, and notes which questions theologians still leave open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deism:
A long entry defines deism as the tendency of thought and criticism that appeared chiefly in England late in the seventeenth century, though French, German, pagan, Jewish, and Muslim deists also existed. Its writers, often called freethinkers, cast off authoritative religious teaching for free rational speculation, and cannot be grouped as one school or one system.

Many were frankly materialistic, and French thinkers building on English deism were almost wholly so. Others kept a religion of nature. The entry sketches the leading English writers in turn: Herbert of Cherbury, Blount, Toland, Shaftesbury, Collins, Woolston, Tindal, Morgan, Chubb, Bolingbroke, Annet, and Dodwell. Each receives his doctrines, methods, and chief works, showing a movement united less by positive teaching than by critical attitude toward revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-determinism:
A philosophy entry on determinism, the theory, named widely since Mill, that every act of will is fixed by earlier conditions. It stands against free will in two main forms. Biological and materialistic versions trace each choice to the body's physical state, while psychological versions trace it to character joined with the motives pressing at the moment.

Supporters reject the labels of necessarianism and fatalism, which hint at outside compulsion, and stress only steady sequence between motive and choice. Opponents answer that the self itself causes volition, freely and from within. If determinism held, the entry argues, responsibility, merit, sin, and reward would turn illusory, and ethics itself would fall.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modernism: Modernism was the early-1900s movement that tried to reconcile Catholicism with modern criticism, and Pius X condemned it as the synthesis of all heresies in 1907. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-molinism: Molinism is the Jesuit theory that reconciles God's grace with human freedom through His knowledge of what we would freely do. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monasticism: Monasticism is the life of prayer apart from the world, and this entry surveys its whole history: the desert fathers, Benedict, the medieval orders, and the modern revivals. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monism: Monism claims that all reality is one substance, and this entry examines its forms, from materialist to idealist, against the Catholic doctrines of God, soul, and matter. A systematic critique in the scholastic style. The one and the many, philosophically weighed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monophysites-: The Monophysites taught that Christ has only one nature, and their rejection of Chalcedon split the Eastern Church permanently. This entry explains the doctrine, its national churches, and the centuries of controversy. The heresy that became a communion: its churches survive in Egypt, Syria, and Armenia today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monotheism: Monotheism is the belief in one God, and this entry traces its history: Israel's revelation, philosophy's approaches, and the religions that claim it. A compact account of humanity's greatest religious idea, from Abraham to the philosophers who reasoned their way to one God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mormonism: Mormonism began with Joseph Smith's golden plates in 1830 and became one of America's most distinctive religions. This entry surveys its history, doctrines, and polygamous past from the Catholic perspective. The American-born faith, examined from outside: the entry traces its rise from Palmyra to Utah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mysticism: Mysticism is the soul's direct experience of God, and this entry surveys its history, its psychology, and its great witnesses across the Christian centuries. The heart of religion, examined with care: the entry weighs its psychology, its dangers, and its fruits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naturalism: Naturalism denies the supernatural and makes nature the whole of reality. This entry examines its forms, its arguments, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy that closes heaven: the entry answers its claims point by point with scholastic rigor and clarity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naturism: Naturism is the worship of nature itself, and this entry traces its forms from primitive animism to modern pantheism. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-platonism: Neo-Platonism was the last great philosophy of antiquity, Plotinus's vision of all reality flowing from the One. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-scholasti: Neo-Scholasticism was the 19th-century revival of Aquinas, blessed by Leo XIII's Aeterni Patris in 1879. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nestorius-and: Nestorius denied that Mary is the Mother of God, and the Council of Ephesus condemned him in 431. This entry explains his doctrine, his trial, and the far-flung Nestorian church that carried Christianity to China. The heresy that reached the Pacific.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nihilism: Nihilism was the Russian creed that denied everything, from God to morality to the state. This entry examines its origins, its doctrines, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy of the void: its bombs shook the tsar's empire in the 1800s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nominalism-re: Do universals exist? Nominalists said no, realists said yes, and conceptualists split the difference, in the great medieval debate. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-novatian-and-: Novatian was the rigorist antipope whose schism refused forgiveness to the lapsed, and his sect lasted for centuries. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occasionalism: Occasionalism teaches that God alone truly causes anything, with creatures as mere occasions. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occult-art-oc: Occultism is the claim to hidden powers and secret knowledge, from magic to theosophy. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ontologism: Ontologism taught that we see God directly in every act of knowing, and Rome condemned it. This entry explains the system, its authors, and its censure. The philosophy that looked too high: Rome condemned its claim to see God directly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-optimism: Optimism is the doctrine that this is the best of all possible worlds, taught by Leibniz. This entry explains the system, its arguments, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy of the best: the entry answers Voltaire's mocking Candide with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-origen-and-or: Origen was the dazzling Alexandrian whose genius shaped Christian theology and whose errors were condemned. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paganism: Paganism is the world of the old gods, and this long entry surveys its religions, its philosophy, and its encounter with the Gospel. The darkness before the dawn: the entry maps the old gods' vast and varied ancient dominion fully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palm-in-chris: The palm is the Christian symbol of victory, laid before martyrs and the triumphant Christ. This entry traces its use in art, liturgy, and the catacombs. The tree of the conquerors: its branches crowned the martyrs and holy virgins alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panpsychism: Panpsychism is the doctrine that all things have some degree of mind or soul. This entry explains the theory, its forms, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy that thinks everything thinks: the entry traces it from the ancient Greek philosophers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pantheism: Pantheism identifies God with the universe, and this entry examines its forms from the Stoics to Spinoza, with the Catholic refutation. The error that drowns God in the world: the entry refutes its bold claims quite systematically and fully here.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parallelism: Parallelism is the rhyming of thoughts that makes Hebrew poetry sing, line answering line. This entry explains its forms, its beauty, and its use. The psalms' native music: their parallel lines still sing so sweetly in every single human tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelagius-and-: Pelagius denied original sin and made man his own savior, and Augustine crushed his heresy. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pessimism: Pessimism is the philosophy that life is not worth living. This entry examines its systems, from Schopenhauer to Hartmann, and the Catholic answer. The doctrine of despair, refuted: the entry answers it firmly with bright and certain Catholic hope indeed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pestalozzi-an: Pestalozzi was the Swiss educator who taught that love is the soul of teaching. This entry covers his schools, his method, and his Catholic critics. The father of the modern school: his famous Yverdon institute drew the admiring world's gaze.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phenomenalism: Phenomenalism is the philosophy that we know only appearances, never things themselves. This entry examines its systems, from Hume to Mill, and the Catholic critique. The doctrine of the veil of sense: its denial of substance ends in bleak scepticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philanthropin: Philanthropinism was Basedow's 1700s movement to educate children by nature and reason. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietism: Pietism was the Lutheran movement that sought a religion of the heart against dead orthodoxy. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plato-and-pla: Plato's philosophy shaped Christian thought more than any other pagan system. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polytheism: Polytheism is the worship of many gods, humanity's oldest error. This entry examines its forms, its causes, and the Catholic refutation. The many gods that are no gods: their dumb idols fell silent before the fearless preaching of the Gospel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-positivism: Positivism is Comte's system that banished metaphysics for science. This entry examines its doctrines, its religion of humanity, and the Catholic refutation. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poverty-and-p: Poverty and pauperism are the social wounds the Church has always tended. This entry examines their causes, their remedies, and the Catholic teaching. The problem of the poor: its true answer is organized Christian charity in daily action for souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pragmatism: Pragmatism is the philosophy that judges truth by its works. This entry examines its founders, its doctrines, and the Catholic critique. The test of the cash value: its clever pragmatists doubted that the absolute truth itself had ever really existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-predestinaria: Predestinarianism is the heresy that denied man's free will. This entry traces its teachers, its condemnations, and its errors. The denial of the will's freedom: its dark error chained the helpless human soul in iron fate forevermore in hopeless darkness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presbyteriani: Presbyterianism is the Calvinist system of church rule by elders. This entry examines its doctrines, its history, and the Catholic judgment. The kirk of the Scots: its stern General Assembly rules in Edinburgh's High Kirk today still in solemn session.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priscillianis: Priscillianism was the Spanish heresy of the fourth century. This entry traces its doctrines, its councils, and its condemnation. The ascetic heresy of the West: its condemned bishops died at Trier in 385's cold autumn winds of Gaul's far frontier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-probabilism: Probabilism is the moral system that follows a probable opinion. This entry examines its doctrine, its defenders, and its opponents. The liberty of the doubtful conscience: its great masters were the learned Jesuits of olden days gone by in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protestantism: Protestantism is the great schism of the sixteenth century. This long entry examines its origins, its divisions, and the Catholic judgment. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psycho-physic: Psycho-physical parallelism is the theory that mind and body run side by side. This entry examines its forms and the Catholic critique. The two clocks of the soul: their twin hands never truly touch in the theory's rigid scheme of mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pusey-and-pus: Puseyism was the Oxford Movement's Catholic revival. This entry traces Pusey's life, the Tracts, and the Catholic judgment. The high church road to Rome: its famous Tracts stirred sleepy Oxford's dons to anger and learned debate in print and pulpit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pyrrhonism: Pyrrhonism is the ancient philosophy of universal doubt. This entry examines its founder, its tropes, and the Catholic refutation. The suspension of all judgment: its smiling sage doubted everything in life and in thought alike in ancient Elis of Greece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pythagoras-an: Pythagoras was the sage of numbers and the transmigrating soul. This entry examines his life, his school, and his influence. The philosopher of the harmony: his great theorem rules the schools of geometry today still unchallenged in proof and use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quietism: Quietism is the heresy of passive prayer that abandoned effort. This entry traces Molinos, its condemnation, and its errors. The rest that renounced the will: its condemned errors died in 1687's papal decree Coelestis Pastor forevermore in Rome itself in print.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rationalism: Rationalism is the philosophy that enthroned reason above faith. This entry examines its forms, its masters, and the Catholic refutation. The revolt of the unaided mind: its proud systems denied the Christian mysteries of faith and grace and hope and heaven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relativism: Relativism is the doctrine that truth changes with the mind. This entry examines its forms and the Catholic refutation. The philosophy of the shifting standard: its crooked measure bends with fickle men and changing times and moods and fashions and whims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-ind: Religious indifferentism is the error that all faiths are equal. This entry examines its forms and the Catholic condemnation. The denial of the one true Church: its proud error levels the faiths of men in folly and pride and blindness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ritschlianism: Ritschlianism is the theology of Albrecht Ritschl's school. This entry examines its doctrines and the Catholic refutation. The kingdom without the King: its cold ethics displaced the dogma of Christ the Lord and God and Man and Savior and King.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-catechi: The Roman Catechism is the Trent's manual for parish priests. This entry examines its origin, its doctrine, and its influence. The book of the Council's mind: its weighty pages teach the priests of the world in Latin and the vernacular.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rosmini-and-r: Antonio Rosmini was the philosopher-priest of Rovereto. This entry examines his system, his condemnation, and his vindication. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatarians-: The Sabbatarians are the keepers of the Saturday Sabbath. This entry examines their sects, their doctrines, and the Catholic judgment. The observers of the seventh day: their scattered sects keep the Saturday Sabbath in the 1600s' England of the Civil War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-simon-a: Saint-Simon was the prophet of the industrial order. This entry examines his doctrine, his disciples, and the Church's judgment. The utopian of the new Christianity: his ardent school dreamed the future in Paris in the 1820s' salons of the left.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scepticism: Scepticism is the doubt of the knowable. This long entry examines its kinds, its history, and the Church's answer. The philosophy of the suspended judgment: its cold doubt questions all in the schools of the age in the 1700s' salons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schism: Schism is the rent in the Church's unity. This long entry examines its nature, its kinds, and its history. The separation of the disobedient: its sad rent divides the flock in the Church of Christ in schism's wound in the body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scholasticism: Scholasticism is the philosophy of the schools. This very long entry examines its method, its masters, and its history. The reasoned faith of the Middle Ages: its great masters crowned Paris in the 1200s' schools of the university in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secularism: Secularism is the creed of the world without God. This entry examines its doctrines, its prophets, and the Church's answer. The philosophy of the closed horizon: its cold creed denies the altar in the 1800s' schools of the West in the cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semiarians-an: The Semiarians were the half-way Arians. This entry examines their creeds, their councils, and their end. The heresy of the middle party: its wavering creeds died in the 300s in the East's councils in the provinces of the empire in Asia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semipelagiani: Semipelagianism is the error of the half-grace. This entry examines its doctrines, its monks, and its condemnation. The heresy of the Marseilles theologians: its subtle error died in the 500s in Gaul's monasteries in the south of the province in Lérins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shamanism: Shamanism is the religion of the spirit-men. This entry examines its rites, its peoples, and its errors. The sorcery of the northern tribes: its wild drums call the spirits in the steppes of Asia in the north of the continent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sikhism: Sikhism is the religion of the Punjab's Gurus. This entry examines its ten masters, its book, and its creed. The faith of the Khalsa brotherhood: its ten Gurus taught the Punjab in the 1500s' villages in the north of India.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socialism: Socialism is the creed of the common ownership. This long entry examines its schools, its errors, and the Church's judgment. The doctrine of the collectivist state: its many schools filled the 1800s in Europe's cities in the factories of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socinianism: Socinianism is the heresy of the Polish Brethren. This entry examines its doctrines, its Racovian, and its end. The anti-Trinitarians of the Reformation: their famed catechism filled Raków in the 1600s' Poland in the Commonwealth of the nobles in the sejm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritism: Spiritism is the traffic with the dead. This entry examines its séances, its errors, and the Church's judgment. The fraud of the darkened room: its turning tables filled the 1850s in the salons of the credulous in the cities of the West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritualism: Spiritualism is the philosophy of the spirit's primacy. This entry examines its schools, its doctrines, and its errors. The idealism of the modern mind: its many schools filled the 1800s in the universities of the West in the faculties of the mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-symbolism: Symbolism is the language of sacred signs. This long entry examines its liturgy, its art, and its meaning. The speech of the veiled mysteries: its holy signs filled the liturgy in the 400s of the Church in the basilicas of the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syncretism: Syncretism is the mixture of religions. This entry traces its philosophy and its danger. The blending of the incompatible faiths: its grave errors filled the apologetics in the 200s of the Fathers in the books of the very old apologists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syndicalism: Syndicalism is the movement of the trade unions. This entry traces its Sorel, its strikes, and its doctrine. The revolt of the working class: its great strikes filled the factories in the 1900s' France in the towns of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taoism: Taoism is the religion of the Way. This long entry examines its Laozi, its immortals, and its history. The philosophy of the Chinese sages: its mystic Way crowned the mountains in the 400s BC of the sages in the valleys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-lamb-in-e: The Lamb is the symbol of Christ. This entry traces its catacombs, its Agnus, and its meaning. The emblem of the sacrificed Lord: its carved form crowned the catacombs in the 100s of the martyrs in the very old tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomism: Thomism is the school of Aquinas. This very long entry examines its 1200s, its Summa, and its history. The philosophy of the Angelic Doctor: its great Summa crowned Paris in the 1270s of the Dominicans in the very old schools.
darwiniana-essays-and-reviews-pertaining:
Asa Gray's Darwiniana, printed at New York in 1876, collects the Harvard botanist's essays and reviews on Darwin's theory. Gray held the Fisher professorship of natural history, and his first article reviews the Origin of Species itself. Species, variation, and artificial selection receive a botanist's definitions. Agassiz, his Harvard colleague and Darwin's great opponent, stands opposite throughout.

Design versus Necessity and Natural Selection Not Inconsistent with Natural Theology argue Gray's lifelong position: evolution by natural selection can be theistic. Later articles follow De Candolle on oaks and Falconer on elephants. Gray arranged Darwin's American reception more than any other man, defending the science and reconciling it with faith. The volume is primary evidence in the Victorian debate, written by the friend Darwin trusted with his American defence. Its calm tone is itself an argument.
doe-osti-2997177-operational-forecasting: Predicting human-caused earthquakes got its DOE forecaster, and this CRADA final tunes the warning system. The pages log the prediction trials. The geophysicists get their closeout. The quakes were induced. The trials were prediction. The closeout was geophysicist. The system was warning.
doe-osti-3018774-feasibility-and-qualita: Fuel cell buses got airport-backup-assessed, and this DOE text studies emergency power. The pages detail the risk findings. The transport folks get their data. The use was backup power. The data were transport. The power was emergency. The assessment was risk.
doe-osti-3409108-the-hawaii-meteorology-: Hawaii MET got toolkit-built, and this DOE toolkit covers meteorology energy transmission. The pages detail the Hawaii findings. The energy folks get their data. The toolkit was transmission. The data were energy. The MET were Hawaii. The transmission were toolkit.
english-literary-criticism:
English Literary Criticism, by Charles Edwyn Vaughan and edited by C H Herford, sketches how criticism grew in England. Vaughan states his aim in the preface. He will trace the development of critical method. Each phase will be illustrated by samples from its most typical writers. He has not tried, he says, to collect the most striking pieces in the literature. The last sixty years are too rich for full treatment.

One specimen of one modern writer must suffice. That writer is Walter Pater, the critic many judge the most remarkable of all. Vaughan closes the volume with Pater's essay on the painter Sandro Botticelli. A study of painting may seem a strange end for literary criticism. Vaughan defends it: modern criticism dissolves the wall between poetry and painting. The anthology runs from the earliest English critics to that border crossing.
govdocs-archive_org-VealeFJPAdvanceToBar:
F. J. P. Veale, an English solicitor and writer, published Advance to Barbarism to trace how warfare became total between Sarajevo and Hiroshima. His span runs from the First World War's opening shots to the atomic bombing of Japan in 1945.

Veale argues that modern war shed its old limits step by step, until bombing cities and killing civilians became normal practice, and he lays much of the blame on the Allied side. The book became a staple of revisionist history and is still hotly debated. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers weighing its charges.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Patriotism_Patr: Titled simply 'Patriotism,' this declassified US government document sits in the Internet Archive's govdocs set. What it says about patriotism - or who wrote it, and when - the catalog does not say. No public text has been located. A title in search of its contents.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Vandalism_Vanda: nsia-Vandalism Vandalism: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
mediaeval-socialism:
Bede Jarrett wrote Mediaeval Socialism, printed in London and New York. Jarrett was a Dominican friar, marked by the initials O.P. Seven chapters and a book list make up the short work.

An intro sets the scene, then social conditions in the middle ages. Chapters treat the communists, the schoolmen, and the lawyers of that age. Social reformers get a chapter of their own near the end. The last chapter weighs the old theory of giving alms to the poor. A full index closes the book for students who cite it. Jarrett writes as both a friar and a trained scholar.
mill-utilitarianism:
John Stuart Mill published Utilitarianism in 1863, his clear short statement of the moral theory he inherited from Jeremy Bentham and his father. The book first ran as essays in Fraser's Magazine in 1861. Mill meant it as the theory's best case, not a textbook.

The creed is simple: acts are right as they add to happiness, wrong as they add to pain. Mill answers the stock attacks: that the rule is a pig's philosophy, too cold, or too hard to use. He ranks pleasures of mind above those of body, and grounds justice in utility. The book remains the theory's standard statement.
moulton-early-zoroastrianism:
James Hope Moulton's Early Zoroastrianism appeared in 1913 as Hibbert Lectures. The Manchester scholar gives the classic English study of the prophet. Zoroaster's faith, among the oldest prophetic faiths, fills his pages.

Moulton traces the Gathas, the hymns held to be Zoroaster's own words. The stark duel of good and evil stands at the faith's core. He weighs the faith's long sway on Jews, Christians, and others. Learning sits lightly in prose a plain reader can follow with ease. Many still call the book the best first guide to the whole subject. Moulton's fairness toward a faith not his own wins trust fast.
nasa-tm-19650024111-dipole-resonances-in:
Peter A Sturrock, of Ames Research Center and Stanford's Institute for Plasma Research, studied resonances in a magnetized plasma. Radar soundings from a satellite above the ionosphere had shown such resonances. A dipole antenna can excite them and can also detect them. A plasma is resonant, Sturrock explains, when the group velocity for a mode falls to zero.

His treatment is theoretical and treats the dipole as vanishingly small. The plasma is taken as uniform, or homogeneous, throughout. Ionosphere soundings from satellites were new at the time. Explaining their odd echoes required exactly this kind of careful wave theory, tied to a real instrument in orbit.
nasa-tm-19690009834-the-sdp-3-a-computer:
R. A. Cliff of Goddard Space Flight Center describes the SDP-3, a computer built for small scientific spacecraft, in this paper. Spacecraft radios can only send limited data to Earth. Cliff argues for raising the worth of each transmitted bit instead of just sending more bits.

The SDP-3 is a general-purpose stored-program computer meant as the core of a small spacecraft data system. It processes data on board and removes redundancy before transmission. Removing redundancy in space can use less power than sending the raw data. The machine uses serial, two's complement arithmetic with sixteen-bit words. A sixteen-level priority interrupt system supports time-sharing operation aboard the spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19690025525-the-feasibility-of-w:
William J. Robinson Jr., of the Space Sciences Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this revised report, TM X-53806, dated May 27, 1969. He studies the feasibility of beaming power wirelessly to an orbiting astronomical station. A station fed from outside could avoid carrying all of its own power generation gear into orbit.

Two beaming methods are worked through in full: microwaves and lasers. For each, Robinson covers power generation, transmission across space, and reception with conversion back to electricity. Overall microwave efficiencies get their own summary section. A head-to-head comparison then weighs the two methods stage by stage. Artist's drawings show the station under each kind of beam before the conclusions chapter.
paradoxes-of-catholicism:
Robert Hugh Benson's Paradoxes of Catholicism began as sermons. He preached them in England and in New York. A complete course followed in Rome, in the Lent of 1913. His preface, dated Easter 1913, warns that the pages abbreviate the sermons. Some ideas appeared earlier in Christ in the Church. He risked repetition rather than incoherency, he says.

The contents pair opposites throughout. Jesus Christ, God and Man, opens the course. The Catholic Church, Divine and Human, follows. Peace and War, Wealth and Poverty, and Sanctity and Sin come next. Joy and Sorrow, Faith and Reason, and Authority and Liberty continue the pattern. Benson, a convert and a priest, argues that the Church holds both poles of each pair at once.
plato-and-platonism: Walter Pater's Plato and Platonism reaches this library as a Project Gutenberg e-text, number 4095 in that series, produced by Alfred J. Drake. The sample held for this entry, however, contains only the Project Gutenberg header and license matter, with the title and author's name, and no pages of Pater's text itself. Because the sample shows no part of the work's actual writing, its treatment of Plato cannot be described from the evidence provided here.
podcast-dannyjones-8jksrbKGGSM:
Travis Kitchens returns to Danny Jones's podcast with a claim pitched at full volume. Billionaires, he says, are secretly funding a psychedelic holy war. In his account they bankroll the spread of mind-altering drugs as a spiritual and political project. Kitchens connects foundations, research money, and the psychedelic revival into one design.

Jones works through the money trail with him, name by name. The revival itself is real and well funded, and readers can verify its donors; the holy war framing is Kitchens's interpretation of that money's purpose. The episode keeps the two separate in presentation even when the guest merges them. For listeners tracking how psychedelics moved from counterculture to boardrooms, the conversation offers a suspicious, detailed, and arguable map of who paid for the trip.
podcast-dannyjones-JMR7_5SSWsM:
Whitley Strieber wrote Communion, the bestselling account of his own abduction experiences, and changed how America pictured aliens. With Danny Jones, the most famous abduction witness alive discusses human-alien hybrids said to live among us, and what he believes the visitors intend for humanity.

Strieber has told his story for nearly forty years, refining a theology of the encounter along the way. Jones questions him as a seeker rather than a skeptic, and Strieber answers with the calm of a man long past caring who believes him. No evidence settles his claims, and the episode offers testimony instead. Its preservation value is cultural: the founding witness of the modern abduction era, speaking at length in his own late style, for the audience that inherited his imagery.
podcast-dannyjones-j_gMP1TgFsM:
Con artist Matthew Cox joins Danny Jones for a true-crime talk billed around the Gabby Petito case. The title asks if her fiance was a psychopath. Cox knows fraud and prison from the inside.

The sample opens on Cox's own new film about a con man contest in Europe. It then turns to the Theranos trial of Elizabeth Holmes. Cox gives a fraudster's read on lies, charm, and self-belief. The Petito question frames the hour, but Cox's own past gives the talk its sharp, uneasy edge throughout. Listeners get both crime analysis and showmanship.
podcast-joerogan-cdP3L73yySM:
Commentator Hotep Jesus sits with Rogan for episode 1318 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Known for blunt online broadcasts, he brings an unfiltered take on race, culture, and the internet's wars. The talk is fiery by design, and Rogan lets it run hot.

The two argue and joke their way across the subjects that built his following, from media narratives to personal responsibility. Rogan pushes back where the claims stretch and laughs where they land. The episode preserves a provocative voice at full volume, the kind of guest booking that made the young show a free-speech landmark for its fans.
podcast-joerogan-p6LJXPOv4SM:
Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sits with Joe Rogan for episode 1999, recorded while Kennedy was running for president. Kennedy, an environmental lawyer from the famous political family, had broken with the Democratic Party. The long talk gave his campaign one of its biggest platforms.

Kennedy lays out his views on vaccines, public health agencies, and corporate power over government. He also talks about the environment and the legacy of his father and uncle, both killed in the 1960s. Rogan lets him speak at length with few interruptions. The episode became a key moment in Kennedy's run and in Rogan's political reach.
podcast-joerogan-qSLs1-KwasM:
Graham Hancock returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2215 with fresh claims about a lost Ice Age civilization. Hancock, author of Fingerprints of the Gods, argues that a comet strike wiped out an advanced culture. His Netflix series made that case to millions.

Hancock updates Rogan on sites and finds he says support his theory. He attacks the archaeology establishment for refusing to debate him fairly. Rogan, his most loyal platform, lets him lay out the full argument at length. The episode shows how Hancock's once-fringe ideas now reach a mass audience first.
podcast-tuckercarlson-tFM6L6TopsM:
Political strategist Steve Bannon joins Tucker Carlson after Israel strikes Iran. Both men oppose deeper American involvement in the war. They warn the fight could split the movement that backed Donald Trump.

Bannon argues that a long war would drain support among working-class voters. Carlson agrees that foreign wars have hurt past presidents and parties. They discuss pressure from donors, media voices, and party leaders. The episode captures a sharp split inside the American right over Israel, Iran, and the limits of loyalty to Trump. Neither man hides how deep his doubts about the war run.
poems-of-american-patriotism:
Brander Matthews chose the poems for this anthology of American patriotic verse, illustrated by N. C. Wyeth and dedicated to the memory of Theodore Roosevelt. Matthews explains in his preface, first written in New York in 1882 and extended for this revised edition. That he gathered poems of feeling as well as action, since both show the temper of their times. Arrangement is chronological, so that the history of America as told by her poets unfolds in order.

Old favorites dominate, printed carefully from the best texts, with brief notes before many poems explaining the occasion that produced them. Two score years of new events forced changes for the extended edition, dropping a few lesser pieces to make room for recent commemorations. The result is a nation's story in song, from colonial daring to modern war, as its own poets chose to sing it.
poems-of-optimism:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox issued Poems of Optimism in 1913, and the London edition of 1919 from Gay and Hancock shows a book transformed by war. Her usual creed, that attitude conquers circumstance, here meets the Great War head-on. The contents open with a whole war section: Greater Britain, Belgium, Knitting, Mobilisation, and the Ghosts, poems written while Europe burned and America debated its part.

Wilcox's optimism was never mere smiling; it was a discipline she preached to millions of newspaper readers, and the war poems test it against casualty lists. Poems about the men-made gods and the poet's theme widen the lens from battle to belief. Reprinted in 1915, 1918, and 1919, the volume records how America's favorite encourager answered the worst news of her lifetime, refusing despair in public, in rhyme, on schedule.
pragmatism:
D. L. Murray wrote this short Pragmatism for the series Philosophies Ancient and Modern, with a preface by F. C. S. Schiller, the Oxford humanist who led the movement in Britain. The first chapter, the Genesis of Pragmatism, begins by mocking the newspapers' picture of the doctrine: audacious novelty. An insurgence of emotion against logic, transatlantic slang, the sordid commercialism of the Anglo-Saxon mind dressed as philosophy.

All these ideas are mistaken, Murray answers. Pragmatism is neither revolt nor revolution but evolution, a collective name for the most modern solution of puzzles that have impeded philosophy from time immemorial. As interesting to common sense as to the metaphysician. His exposition tests the doctrine against skepticism since Hume and against the part that will plays in accepting beliefs. As an introduction written while the fight was live, the book has the advantage of explaining pragmatism before the textbooks froze it.
preaching-and-paganism:
Albert Parker Fitch, professor of the history of religion at Amherst College. Delivered these lectures as the forty-sixth series of the Lyman Beecher lectureship on preaching at Yale, published by Yale University Press in 1920. The title states his provocation: the church that means to preach to a modern age must first understand how much of that age is honestly pagan. How much of its own preaching has forgotten what religion is.

Fitch had already asked whether the church can survive in the changing order, and this volume presses the question on the preachers themselves. The Cooper memorial fund, honoring a Connecticut pastor of the class of 1865, carried the lectures into print. The book belongs to the moment when American Protestantism, shaken by war and science. Debated whether to fight modernity or to baptize it, and Fitch argues for preaching that knows its audience's real creed.
sextus-empiricus-and-greek-scepticism:
Mary Mills Patrick, president of the American College at Constantinople, wrote this study as a thesis taken for a doctor's degree at the University of Bern in November 1897. Deighton Bell issued it at Cambridge in 1899. A list of German studies of Sextus by Pappenheim opens the scholarly frame.

Patrick pairs her study of Greek doubt with her own English version of the first book of Sextus Empiricus's Pyrrhonic Sketches. Sextus set out the sceptics' way of withholding assent from all claims. Readers meet both a careful account of that school and a primary text in which its method speaks for itself.
the-essence-of-buddhism:
The Essence of Buddhism, pocket series number 325 from E. Haldeman-Julius at Girard, Kansas, copyrighted in 1922, is a Buddhist anthology. Its preface praises the plan: cut and uncut jewels of wisdom, compassion, and human brotherhood, culled from many Buddhist sources by Mr. Bowden. One such gem worn on the heart, the preface says, would enrich a day.

Bowden disclaims any full corpus of doctrine or morals. Short texts and tales let new readers taste the faith in cheap, plain form. The ten-cent format put world religion in a coat pocket.
the-heavenly-father-lectures-on-modern-a:
Ernest Naville, late professor of philosophy in the University of Geneva, wrote The Heavenly Father, lectures on modern atheism. The book was translated from the French by Henry Downton, M.A., English chaplain at Geneva, and published in Boston in 1867. A quoted line states the aim: to oppose error with faith in God as given by the Gospel, faith in the Heavenly Father.

The preface explains that the lectures were first delivered at Geneva and then at Lausanne, before two audiences that together numbered about two thousand five hundred men. Portions taken down in shorthand ran in a Swiss review. Readers in other countries then sought translations, and proof sheets were sent out as the work came from the press.
the-inhumanity-of-socialism:
Edward F. Adams joined two papers in this volume. One was read at the University of California in 1913. The League of the Republic heard it there. An earlier one went to the Ruskin Club of Oakland. His foreword concedes a hard point. A lifetime of writing on socialism would say nothing new. Each new age still wants fresh statements, he argues. Old texts do not satisfy new readers.

His own position is absolute. Socialism is inhuman, he argues. It saps the vigor of the human race. It lulls strugglers into sloth. It stops enterprise and rewards poor work. It breeds hatred and checks production. It feeds the poor hopes that cannot come true. His closing motto urges respect for law. It praises regard for the rights of others. It counsels contentment with the simple life. The book is a period piece of American argument.
the-junior-classics-volume-7-stories-of-: Volume seven of The Junior Classics covers Stories of Courage and Heroism. William Patten selected the set, Charles W. Eliot wrote its introduction, and William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. A picture of Catherine Douglas fronts it, thrusting her arm through a door's empty staples. Only the title pages and first contents page are present here. The stories themselves do not appear. The list opens with Beatrice Harraden on Phidias. Charlotte M. Yonge treats Thermopylae and Regulus. Saint Genevieve follows. Jacob Abbott covers Caesar crossing the Rubicon.
the-practice-and-theory-of-bolshevism: Bertrand Russell's The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism was first published in London by George Allen and Unwin in November 1920 and reprinted in February 1921. The front pages shown here carry a transcriber's note, the title page, and the contents. Part I, on the present condition of Russia, lists chapters on what is hoped from Bolshevism and on general characteristics. A chapter on Lenin, Trotsky, and Gorky follows, then art and education. The part closes with communism and the Soviet constitution. The chapters themselves are not shown.
the-soul-of-man-under-socialism:
An essay on socialism and individual freedom, printed in London by Arthur L. Humphreys, argues that the chief gain from socialism would be release from the sordid necessity of living for others. A transcribed note credits the text to a Humphreys edition, and no author's name is printed on the title pages present here.

The writer concedes that rare figures such as Darwin, Keats, Renan, and Flaubert managed to stand apart and perfect what was in them, to the world's lasting gain. Most people, though, spoil their lives through exaggerated altruism, moved by surrounding poverty and starvation. Their well-meant remedies, the essay charges, merely prolong the disease they hope to cure, beginning with attempts to solve poverty by keeping the poor alive.
the-story-of-mormonism-and-the-philosoph:
James E. Talmage, a doctor of science, wrote these two linked works, and the publishers' preface from Salt Lake City, dated March 1914, explains their history. The Story began as lectures. Talmage delivered them at the University of Michigan, Cornell University, and elsewhere. They were first printed in the Improvement Era as a report of the lectures. A booklet from the Millennial Star office in Liverpool followed.

A revised edition from the Bureau of Information in 1910 recast the lecture style into ordinary essay form, and this third American edition is revised and amplified again. The Philosophy began as a lecture before the Philosophical Society of Denver, and translations of both works had already appeared in Swedish, Greek, Russian, Danish, and German in response to steady demand.
unitarianism:
W. G. Tarrant wrote this short history of Unitarianism, printed at London in 1912. His contents trace the movement in two lands. Early chapters cover the Unitarian martyrs of England, the old nonconformists, and the tracts that spread the cause. A New England section runs from the years before the Great Awakening to the liberal reaction that followed it.

Later parts take up the legal recognition of English Unitarianism, questions of inheritance of chapels and funds, and the modern movement's communities, ideas, and teaching methods. Tarrant opens by explaining his key terms. He says the chief issue between Trinitarians and Unitarians comes first, so that a reader can follow the history with the main dispute clear in mind. The book serves as a compact map of a small church with a long past.
what-is-darwinism: Only the title page and contents list are shown here, so Hodge's argument itself does not appear. Charles Hodge of Princeton wrote What Is Darwinism?, printed in New York in 1874. The contents open with the weight of the question. He then sets out views on how the world and living things began, naming scriptural, pantheist, and Epicurean views. Herbert Spencer gets his own part. Later parts turn to Darwin's theory, natural selection, and what Darwin means by the word natural.
